bridge: F01 introduced memory corruption. Compare protections against a known local example rather than assuming that a label means complete safety.
teaching:
### Match each protection with its job

Address-space layout randomisation, or ASLR, varies locations to make useful addresses harder to predict. Non-executable memory aims to stop instructions being run from regions meant for data. A stack canary places a check value to detect some overwrites before returning.

These mechanisms address different exploitation steps. None automatically prevents every out-of-bounds access or incorrect program decision.

### Understand control-flow protection

Control-flow integrity restricts certain transfers of execution to permitted destinations under a policy. The strength of that policy and the operations it covers matter. A broad set of permitted targets may leave more room than a narrow one.

### Consider prevention as well as mitigation

Memory-safe languages and safe interfaces can remove classes of invalid access. Their guarantees still depend on unsafe code, foreign-library boundaries and implementation details. A language choice does not automatically fix access-control or business-logic errors.

### Interpret a changed result carefully

If a protection turns a local overwrite into a detected crash, that is a useful observed difference. Report what was blocked and under which build settings. Continue to fix the original invalid access and check normal behaviour.

In particular, a memory-safe application may call unsafe native libraries. Inspect those boundaries and their ownership rules rather than assuming the calling language automatically protects every library operation.
example:
Fault: write 9 bytes into an 8-byte object.
Bounds check: rejects before write -> addresses root cause.
NX: may block execution from a data page -> write can still corrupt data.
ASLR: changes addresses -> does not make 9 fit into 8.
Canary: may detect some overwrites -> layout/path dependent.
Memory-safe container: enforces bounds under its supported operations.
explanation: The key arithmetic remains wrong under all layout mitigations. Data-only corruption may matter even when injected code cannot execute. A useful report explains the remaining consequence rather than dismissing a bug because one exploit technique is harder.
exercise: Create a table for all five example controls: bounds checking, NX, ASLR, canary and a memory-safe container. For each give its prevention/detection/hardening role, assumption and one remaining risk. For one selected mitigation describe how the supported lab would inspect actual build/runtime evidence, without attempting an exploit. Paper plans must be labelled unperformed.
solution: Bounds check: prevents this write if every relevant path checks the true capacity before access; lifetime defects can remain. NX: hardens execution from selected pages if permissions are applied; data corruption remains. ASLR: hardens address prediction if relevant mappings are randomised and not exposed by leaks; the overflow still exists. Canary: detects selected overwrites if the protected marker is checked before return; other objects/paths can be missed. Memory-safe container: prevents unsupported out-of-bounds access under its operation guarantees; unsafe/native interfaces or logic bugs remain. Example verification plan: in the designated Linux lab inspect the target artifact’s stack-execution metadata with the provider’s documented tool and compare it with runtime page permissions. Record platform, binary and actual observations; a build flag or paper prediction alone is not runtime verification.
challenge: A reviewer says “ASLR is enabled, so the overflow is fixed.” Write a precise response and propose both a source repair and a boundary regression test.
challenge_solution: ASLR does not repair the out-of-bounds operation. Check required capacity before copying or use a representation that enforces bounds; test just-below, exact-fit and over-limit input while preserving ordinary successful use.
